newsitem.title: USA: ValuJet relatives demand air safety changes.
newsitem.headline: ValuJet relatives demand air safety changes.

text.p: Relatives of ValuJet crash victims on Wednesday called the crash of Flight 592 "negligence," criticized U.S. aviation regulators and demanded changes in air safety rules.

Speaking as a group for the first time since the start of a National Transportation Safety Board hearing into the May 11 crash of Flight 592, which killed all 110 people on board, relatives said their loved ones might have lived had the DC-9 had smoke detectors and extinguishers in the cargo hold.

At a hallway news conference where the NTSB hearing was being held, some of the family members -- who mostly had sat quietly as federal investigators dissected the events leading up to the crash -- spoke angrily about the hearing and the state of U.S. air travel safety.

"This airplane disaster was not pilot error, it was not due to weather. It was due to total negligence and even possible criminal negligence," said Amanda Myers, 44, who lost her mother and father in the crash.

The group of a dozen people issued a list of complaints and demands, saying that airline personnel should be given formal training in the handling of hazardous materials and criticizing the Federal Aviation Administration for not requiring that airlines install fire detection and suppression equipment in aircraft holds.
Investigators suspect hazardous oxygen canisters improperly shipped in Flight 592's cargo hold may have started or fueled a raging fire aboard the plane.
"I am very angry. ValuJet Flight 592 fell out of the sky because of a complete breakdown of the system," Marilyn Chamberlin, mother of pilot Candalyn Kubeck, said.

"ValuJet Flight 592 would not have been lost, even with all the blunders... had there been smoke detectors in the cargo hold. I cannot understand, I will never understand why the FAA has blocked this since 1988," she said.

Some relatives said they also want changes in rules regarding cockpit voice recordings so family members could be allowed to hear the final conversations and sounds aboard the plane. Transcripts of the recordings were released this week, but the tapes themselves have not been.

The relatives also complained of a lack of communication between ValuJet and its contractors, lack of warning labels on hazardous material and lack of tiedowns and nets to hold cargo in plance. They also charged that the FAA's responsibilities to regulate and promote air travel were in conflict.

Some family members called the hearing a publicity event at which the companies involved in the crash, ValuJet and its maintenance contractor, SabreTech, were simply trying to make themselves look good.
"It's very difficult to listen to it," said Katherine Hazen, the widow of co-pilot Richard Hazen.
